title: Canary- and Rollback-Aware Composite Scoring for Predicting Operational Risk of Agentic NetOps Actions: A Confirmatory Null Result
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to evaluate whether a composite canary–rollback scoring metric (combining verifier coverage, canary-simulation pass rate, rollback-success probability, LLM confidence, and abstention utility) predicts simulated runtime outage better than single-factor metrics. Using a deterministic synthetic NetOps task bank and an emulator-based deterministic validator, we evaluated 200 held-out paired tasks (baseline vs. guarded workflow) executed with gpt-5-mini. Pre-registered paired analysis (bootstrap and McNemar exact test) found no difference: both baseline and guarded conditions achieved 200/200 non-outage successes (paired difference = 0.0; 95% CI 0.0–0.0; McNemar p = 1.0). We report the full preregistration, execution manifest, and deterministic artifacts. Interpretation: under the selected synthetic task bank and deterministic validator, the baseline workflow already achieved zero observed outages, preventing the composite score from discriminating risk. We document methodological lessons for future NetOps risk-evaluation studies and enumerate construct, internal, external, and conclusion-validity threats.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows are being proposed to convert operator intent into network configuration changes and limited self-healing actions. Operational adoption requires assurance that model-proposed changes are unlikely to cause outages; common operational safeguards include constraint checking, canary deployment, and rollback mechanisms. Prior work emphasizes generate–verify–repair pipelines and layered verification (e.g., MeshAgent, GVR architectures, SEVER-like verifier mixes) but leaves open how composite, deployment-aware scoring maps to operational outage risk in repeatable evaluations [MeshAgent, Cadenas, Christiansen].
Research question. Can a preregistered composite canary–rollback score predict simulated runtime outage better than any single submetric (verifier pass rate, canary-sim success, rollback probability) when applied to intent-to-configuration tasks in a deterministic emulator? 
Contributions. (1) A machine-readable preregistration (CNSM2026-04-canary-rollback-metrics-v1) specifying task-generation, splits, metrics, estimands, and analysis; (2) an autonomous, deterministic execution of the paired experiment (Npairs=200) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic netops validator; (3) a confirmed null result with complete deterministic artifacts, hashes, and reproducible analysis; (4) a discussion of why the null occurred, practical lessons for NetOps risk metrics, and concrete threats to validity.
sections.related_work:
Verification and generate–verify–repair. Work advocating verification layers between stochastic generation and acceptance (generate–verify–repair/GVR) argues for deterministic oracles to bound risk in regulated settings [Cadenas 2026]. Constraint-guided generation and verifier-anchored agents have been applied to network management to improve reliability and abstention behavior [MeshAgent 2025].
Sequential and cost-aware verification. Operations-research formulations (e.g., SEVER) and queueing-control analyses emphasize that verifier cost, ordering, and token-level drift influence practical verifier design and agent throughput; they motivate composite policies that trade verification cost against residual risk [Christiansen 2026].
Operational readiness and assurance. Recent reviews highlight the gap between detection/diagnosis performance and verified action authority; they recommend closed-loop evaluation that includes canary and rollback artifacts to measure operational risk before granting execution privileges [Adepegba Akintade 2026].
Positioning. Our design combined elements from these threads (constraint validation, canary simulation, rollback trials) and evaluated a composite metric in a preregistered, deterministic paired design using a synthetic task bank and emulator traces. We focus on the discriminative power of a pre-specified composite vs. single-factor baselines under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental plan. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-04-canary-rollback-metrics-v1; preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the disclosure). Key elements: deterministic synthetic NetOps Task Bank v1 with canonicalized intent-to-configuration tasks; deterministic split by hash into train/validation/test (train N=300, val N=100, test N=200 in the preregistration). The primary estimand was the paired difference in episode success rate (guarded − baseline) on the held-out test set; primary confirmatory tests: paired bootstrap (10k resamples pre-registered, seed recorded) and McNemar exact test.
Implementation and execution. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with gpt-5-mini as declared model (execution/model_configuration.json). For each task pair (same seed/intent), a shared initial candidate was generated once and evaluated under two conditions: (a) baseline (direct generation → deterministic validator), (b) guarded (same generation but with guard-layer instrumentation: simulated canary run and rollback success check, composite score computed). The execution manifest records 400 episodes completed (200 paired tasks), 200 model calls used, zero failed episodes, and deterministic scorer outputs (see execution/scoring/*.json). All raw responses, validator traces, and hashed artifacts were stored and included in the public manifest.
Scoring and composite metric. Per preregistration, submetrics were computed deterministically: verifier-coverage fraction, canary-simulation pass (simulated canary applied in emulator), rollback-success probability (scripted fault-injection trials in emulator), LLM-reported confidence, and an abstention-utility proxy. A penalized logistic regression (L2) trained on train+val (as preregistered) produced composite weights; final composite scores were applied to the held-out test. The primary comparison was the paired difference in binary success (no outage) between guarded and baseline conditions.
Analysis. Confirmatory primary analysis used paired-bootstrap percentile CIs (10k resamples, seed 1729) and McNemar exact test on the 2×2 paired contingency table; sensitivity analyses (failed-call treatments, contamination via near-duplicates) were pre-specified and executed deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The autonomous execution completed as planned: 400 episodes (200 paired tasks), 200 model calls, 0 failed episodes; all episodes produced deterministic validator scoring artifacts (execution manifest and analysis artifacts with hashes available). Primary confirmatory outcome (from analysis/results.json): baseline_successes = 200/200, guarded_successes = 200/200; paired contingency: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0.
Primary confirmatory statistics. Paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. The preregistered primary hypothesis (that composite would yield superior AUC-ROC for outage prediction than any single submetric on the held-out test) could not be evaluated in a discriminative sense because no outage labels were observed in either condition on the test set; the composite score had no positive outage examples to separate.
Secondary and sensitivity analyses. No failed-technical episodes occurred; sensitivity analyses (imputations, contamination inclusion) were executed but produced identical results because all episodes were successes. Planned ROC/AUPRC computations are not informative when labels are constant—these were therefore not reported as discriminative evidence. All summary artifacts and contingency tables are included in the artifact manifest (analysis/*.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, hashes recorded).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the null. The preregistered composite scoring architecture and guarded workflow were executed faithfully and deterministically. The observed null (no difference) arises because the baseline direct-generation + deterministic validator pipeline produced zero simulated outages on the selected held-out test tasks under the emulator/validator model. Two non-mutually-exclusive explanations are: (1) the synthetic task bank and the deterministic validator were conservative and easy for the tested generation policy, creating a ceiling effect; (2) the LLM (gpt-5-mini) plus deterministic constraints produced high-quality configurations for the selected intents, so canary/rollback instrumentation had no additional observable benefit in the chosen simulator.
Methodological lessons. (i) When baseline outage prevalence is near zero under the evaluation emulator, discriminative evaluation of risk-prediction metrics is impossible—benchmark and task-bank design must ensure an informative positive-rate of adverse events (or use adversarial/counterfactual perturbations). (ii) Deterministic validators are essential for reproducibility but may underrepresent real-world nondeterminism and environmental faults; introducing calibrated emulator noise or adversarially generated failure modes is necessary for future power to detect metric differences. (iii) Composite metrics must be validated against realistic failure seeds (e.g., partial-op parsing errors, vendor-CLI subtlety) to demonstrate added operational utility.
Operational implication. The null result should not be read as evidence that canary or rollback instrumentation is unnecessary in practice. Rather, it shows that under the chosen synthetic tasks and deterministic validator, baseline generation already satisfied operational constraints. Real deployments with richer failure modes, telemetry noise, and multi-vendor peculiarities may still benefit from composite canary–rollback scoring.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, deterministic paired experiment to test whether a composite canary–rollback risk score improves prediction of simulated outages versus single submetrics. Execution and analysis were completed with full deterministic artifacts. The primary confirmatory result is a null: both baseline and guarded conditions produced 200/200 non-outage successes on the held-out test (paired difference = 0.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]; McNemar p=1.0). The dominant takeaway is methodological: synthetic task-bank design and emulator realism critically determine whether risk-prediction metrics can be meaningfully evaluated. Future work should (a) design failure-rich or adversarial task banks, (b) introduce calibrated nondeterminism and telemetry variability in emulators, and (c) evaluate composite scoring across multiple LLM backends and real-device testbeds to establish external validity. All preregistration, execution artifacts, and deterministic hashes are published with this submission to enable reproducibility and community follow-up.

disclosure_statement: This study was performed autonomously after an autonomy lock that froze the Research Director’s high-level topic constraints (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps). LLM and tooling. The declared model used for execution was gpt-5-mini (see execution/model_configuration.json; model provider: openai_responses). The autonomous orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with deterministic generation semantics and a deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Initial master prompt. The exact immutable initial master-prompt reference is provisioned in the manuscript evidence bundle: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Pre-lock human role. The human Research Director constrained the topic family and approved the autonomy boundary prior to the lock. Collaborative pre-lock development of infrastructure, rehearsals, and tooling occurred; per the master prompt these pre-lock artifacts were excluded as evidence for the final run unless independently recreated by the autonomous pipeline. Autonomy claim. All literature search, research-gap selection, preregistration (CNSM2026-04-canary-rollback-metrics-v1; preregistration SHA-256 recorded in execution_manifest), experiment design freeze, code generation, experiment execution, artifact hashing, analysis, peer-style reviews, manuscript drafting, revisions, compilation checks, and this Disclosure Statement were produced by the autonomous researcher after the lock without manual human editing of technical content. Preregistration and artifacts. The complete machine-readable preregistration, task bank, execution manifest, raw responses, deterministic validator traces, analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, missingness_summary.csv), and artifact hashes are included in the manuscript evidence bundle and referenced by paths and SHA-256 values in the execution manifest. Deviations and failures. The preregistered stopping rules, retry policy, and missingness plans were followed; no technical failures or restarts affecting scientific outcomes occurred (execution_manifest reports failed_episode_count=0). Reproducibility. Deterministic seeds, split-by-hash procedures, and all scoring code paths are recorded. The exact model configuration file path and SHA are in execution/model_configuration.json (artifact hash recorded). Limitations of autonomy. Although the post-lock pipeline was autonomous, the human Research Director selected the domain family and approved the initial master prompt; pre-lock infrastructure development occurred with human collaboration but was not used as primary empirical evidence unless re-generated post-lock. Ethical and safety note. No real devices, proprietary vendor images, or production networks were used; all experiments ran on synthetic tasks and containerized emulators per the preregistered scope.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and deterministic emulator: the tasks and validator may not capture real-world nondeterminism, device heterogeneity, or latent failure modes.
Single-model execution: results reflect gpt-5-mini under the declared adapter; generalization to other LLMs is untested.
Ceiling-effect null result: zero observed outages in both conditions prevented discriminative evaluation of the composite metric on the chosen test set.
Construct validity: simulator-derived outage labels may not map one-to-one to operational outage risk in production networks.
External validity: absence of real-device or multi-vendor proprietary images limits production-readiness claims.
